question: Which HTTP methods are considered safe?

options.text: GET
options.explanation: Correct. GET only reads data and does not change server state. It can be cached by the browser and CDN.

options.text: POST
options.explanation: Incorrect. POST creates a resource — this is a mutation. Each call can create a new object on the server.

options.text: HEAD
options.explanation: Correct. HEAD is GET without the response body. It does not modify data and is used for checking metadata.

options.text: DELETE
options.explanation: Incorrect. DELETE removes a resource — an obvious mutation. It is idempotent, but not safe.

options.text: OPTIONS
options.explanation: Correct. OPTIONS only requests meta-information about allowed methods and does not change server state.

question: You send PUT /tasks/42 with the same request body twice. What happens?

options.text: Two tasks with ID 42 will be created
options.explanation: Incorrect. PUT updates a specific resource by ID; it does not create collections. Two PUTs with the same data produce the same result.

options.text: The resource will be updated twice, possibly causing a version conflict
options.explanation: Incorrect. PUT is idempotent: the second call produces no additional changes compared to the first.

options.text: The result is the same as after the first request — this is idempotent behavior
options.explanation: Correct. PUT is idempotent: replacing a resource with the same data repeatedly does not change the final state.

options.text: The second request will return a 409 Conflict error
options.explanation: Incorrect. 409 occurs on data conflict (e.g., uniqueness violation), not on repeated PUT with the same data.

question: A user updated only the email field in their profile settings. Which method is more appropriate?

options.text: PUT /users/42 with the full user object
options.explanation: Technically works but inefficient: the entire object must be sent. Risk of losing fields the client is unaware of.

options.text: PATCH /users/42 with body { "email": "new@example.com" }
options.explanation: Correct. PATCH is designed for partial updates. Send only the changed fields — the rest remain untouched.

options.text: POST /users/42/update-email with the new email
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is RPC style with a verb in the URL. PATCH exists for resource updates — semantically cleaner and more standard.

options.text: GET /users/42?email=new@example.com
options.explanation: Incorrect. GET is a safe method and must not modify data. Parameters in GET URLs are for filtering, not for mutations.

question: Why does a browser automatically send an OPTIONS request?

options.text: To get a list of all API endpoints
options.explanation: Incorrect. Browsers do not use OPTIONS for API documentation. That is the function of specialized tools (Swagger, Postman).

options.text: CORS preflight: to check if the server allows a cross-domain request
options.explanation: Correct. Before an 'unsafe' cross-origin request (POST, PUT with custom headers), the browser sends OPTIONS and checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

options.text: To check if the server is healthy (health check)
options.explanation: Incorrect. Health checks typically use GET /health or HEAD /health — these are semantically more accurate for this purpose.

options.text: To authorize the user before the main request
options.explanation: Incorrect. Authorization uses the Authorization header or cookies in the main request. OPTIONS does not transmit credentials.

question: What is the difference between PUT and POST when creating a resource?

options.text: With POST, the server assigns the ID; with PUT, the client knows the ID in advance
options.explanation: Correct. POST /tasks creates a task, the server issues an ID. PUT /tasks/uuid creates or replaces a resource with a given ID — upsert behavior.

options.text: POST is idempotent, PUT is not
options.explanation: Incorrect. It is the other way around: PUT is idempotent (repeated request — same result), POST is not idempotent (repeated POST may create a second resource).

options.text: PUT can be used for upsert (create or update)
options.explanation: Correct. PUT /resources/id — if the resource exists, replaces it; if not, creates it. This is standard PUT semantics.

options.text: POST always returns 201, PUT always returns 200
options.explanation: Incorrect. POST on creation returns 201, but this is not a strict rule. PUT may return 201 (creation) or 200 (update) depending on the implementation.
